sources.note: Step 197's consolidation of the KnowledgeOS architecture into an explicit formal state-transition system K=(states,transitions,invariants,lineage), including the eight-component state decomposition, semantic-meaning conservation (I_57), and the CRUD-vs-transition-conditions architectural framing.

rows.anchor: S_t = (I_t,T_t,E_t,K_t,C_t,G_t,A_t,L_t) ... V = {S | I_1(S) AND I_2(S) AND ... AND I_n(S)}. Valid Transition => Invariant Preservation.
rows.statement: Decomposes the complete KnowledgeOS state into eight components (Identity, Temporal, Evidence, Knowledge, Causal, Governance, Authority, Lineage), defines the set of Valid states V as those satisfying all mandatory invariants, and states the fundamental rule that a valid transition must produce a state remaining in V.

rows.anchor: \mathcal{K}=(S,\Tau,I) ... A CRUD model asks: What fields does this object have? Our model asks: Under which conditions may this state become the next state?
rows.statement: Formalizes KnowledgeOS as a state-transition system K=(S,T,I) (states, allowed transitions, invariant set), explicitly contrasted with a conventional CRUD architecture's field-oriented question -- a fundamentally different architectural question about transition conditions rather than object shape.

rows.anchor: State should be reconstructible from authoritative transitions where the domain requires it.
rows.statement: States the deeper, implementation-neutral requirement behind event-sourcing resemblance (S_n=fold(S_0,tau_1..tau_n)): reconstructibility from authoritative transitions is the actual requirement where the domain demands it; KnowledgeOS is not automatically 'an event-sourcing system' by architecture mandate.

rows.anchor: Meaning_A \neq Meaning_B unless a semantic contract establishes correspondence. ... Data preservation does not guarantee semantic preservation.
rows.statement: Introduces conservation of semantic meaning as a distinct concern from data preservation: a concept transmitted to another context may be reinterpreted differently there unless an explicit semantic contract establishes correspondence -- 'data preservation does not guarantee semantic preservation', called possibly the most important lesson from the corpus's four-chapter lens work.

rows.anchor: SemanticCompatibility(M,p) satisfies the receiving context's invariants. Otherwise: TranslatedClaim must remain explicitly marked as transformed.
rows.statement: Defines a semantic mapping M_{A->B} and requires SemanticCompatibility(M,p) to hold against the receiving context's invariants before a claim can be safely transferred; otherwise the transferred claim must remain explicitly marked as a transformed/translated claim.

rows.anchor: I_57: Cross-context knowledge transfer must preserve or explicitly record semantic transformation.
rows.statement: New invariant I_57: cross-context knowledge transfer must preserve semantic meaning or explicitly record any semantic transformation that occurred.

rows.anchor: \mathcal{K}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{I},\mathcal{L}) ... L(S_j)=L(S_i)\cup\{\tau\} for conserved lineage.
rows.statement: Refines the formal transition system to K=(S,T,I,L) (states, transitions, invariants, lineage), with a transition valid when Pre AND Auth AND Evidence AND Policy AND Invariant all hold, and the lineage function recording L(S_j)=L(S_i) union {tau}.

rows.anchor: A governed, provenance-preserving, identity-aware, state-transition system. ... Current state may change; historical lineage must remain reconstructible where the domain requires it. And: Semantic elevation must occur through explicit transitions satisfying invariants.
rows.statement: Step 197 verdict: the architecture has moved from a collection of Knowledge Objects toward a governed, provenance-preserving, identity-aware state-transition system; the two deepest results are that current state may change while historical lineage remains reconstructible where required, and that semantic elevation must occur only through explicit invariant-satisfying transitions.

notations: Eval(P) may be undefined/inaccessible even when P is determinate

sources.note: Candidate principle adapted from Williamson's anti-luminosity argument: an epistemic property can hold without the evaluator being able to determine that it holds (Knowledge(p) not=> Knowledge(Knowledge(p)); Evidence(e) not=> Accessible(e); Rational(p) not=> Known(Rational(p))); gives a formal reason Sat/Eval_c must not be assumed luminous.

rows.anchor: one may not be in a position to know what one's own rational requirements or evidence are. ... Epistemic Property not=> Accessible(Epistemic Property) ... Knowledge(p) not=> Knowledge(Knowledge(p)) ... Eval(P) may be undefined or epistemically inaccessible even when P has a determinate truth value.
rows.statement: States epistemic non-transparency as the strongest single Williamson contribution: an epistemic property (knowledge, evidence, rational requirement) can hold without being accessible to the subject/evaluator, giving a formal reason Sat/Eval_c must not be assumed luminous and must not be confused with truth. Status: [DERIVED - very strong].

rows.anchor: anti-luminosity: roughly, the assumption that whenever a condition obtains, one is automatically in a position to know that it obtains. His argument uses reliability, limited discrimination and sorites-style reasoning. ... EvidenceExists(e) not=> EvaluatorCanEstablish(EvidenceExists(e)) ... Zero(K)=0 not=> Known(Zero(K)=0). This is very important for Zero.
rows.statement: Applies the non-transparency principle specifically to Zero and consistency/completeness: EvidenceExists(e) not=> EvaluatorCanEstablish(EvidenceExists(e)); Consistent(K) not=> Known(Consistent(K)); Complete(K) not=> Known(Complete(K)); Zero(K)=0 not=> Known(Zero(K)=0) -- i.e. even if a knowledge base actually has zero gap, the system may be unable to know that it has zero gap.

rows.anchor: EPISTEMIC LIMITS, ACCESSIBILITY AND KNOWLEDGE STANDING ... EL.1 Factivity [DECIDED/REINFORCED] ... EL.7 Structural Unknowability [PROP — strong research candidate] ... EL.8 Assertion Responsibility [PROP]
rows.statement: Proposes an 8-section theory addition 'EPISTEMIC LIMITS, ACCESSIBILITY AND KNOWLEDGE STANDING': EL.1 Factivity [DECIDED/REINFORCED], EL.2 Epistemic Non-Transparency [DERIVED], EL.3 Knowledge Iteration [DERIVED], EL.4 Evidence Relativity [PROP], EL.5 Margin of Error [PROP], EL.6 Accessibility (distinguishing Truth/Knowability/Accessibility/ActualKnowledge) [DERIVED], EL.7 Structural Unknowability [PROP-strong], EL.8 Assertion Responsibility [PROP], consolidating this file's individual candidates into one proposed section.

rows.anchor: Do not adopt KnowledgeOS = Williamson's epistemology ... Do not adopt Knowledge = Evidence ... He explicitly says the equation does not amount to an analysis of either concept. ... Do not adopt Sat = Knowledge ... Confidence = Margin ... Unknown = Unknowable ... Contr = Epistemic inconsistency ... Zero = Structural unknowability
rows.statement: Explicit rejection list of seven tempting imports: KnowledgeOS=Williamson's-epistemology, Knowledge=Evidence (noting Williamson himself says his E=K thesis is not an analysis of either concept), Sat=Knowledge, Confidence=Margin, Unknown=Unknowable, Contr=EpistemicInconsistency, Zero=StructuralUnknowability -- these remain separate concepts.

rows.anchor: A condition C is defined to be luminous if and only if: For every case alpha, if in alpha C obtains, then in alpha one is in a position to know that C obtains. ... The Sorites-Style Argument [feeling cold at dawn to hot at noon] ... Therefore the condition 'one feels cold' is not luminous.
rows.statement: Gives the formal definition of luminosity (a condition C is luminous iff whenever C obtains one is in a position to know it obtains) and the full sorites-style anti-luminosity argument (feeling-cold-at-dawn-to-hot-at-noon, imperceptible per-step changes) proving virtually no mental state is luminous, including love/hope examples generalizing beyond feeling-cold; grounds the epistemic-non-transparency principle with its original formal source material.

rows.anchor: if we combine the argument with the principle that one is always in a position to know what one's evidence is, the upshot is that one has exactly the same evidence in an ordinary case and its sceptical counterpart. ... Luminous conditions are trivial. Since mental states are non-luminous, the sceptical argument fails. ... KnowledgeOS should not adopt a phenomenal conception of evidence.
rows.statement: Uses non-luminosity to dissolve philosophical scepticism (if evidence were luminous, evidence would be identical between ordinary and sceptical cases, but mental states are non-luminous so the argument fails) and explicitly rejects the phenomenal conception of evidence (a converging-to-the-empty-set sequence of ever-more-private appearances), translated as: KnowledgeOS's evidence must not be modeled as private/phenomenal appearances.

rows.anchor: just as one cannot always know what one's evidence is, so one cannot always know what rationality requires of one. ... rationality is not luminous. ... the system cannot assume that Determination is always accessible.
rows.statement: Extends non-luminosity specifically to rationality (one cannot always know what rationality requires), translated as: KnowledgeOS cannot assume Determination is always accessible/transparent to the system itself.

rows.anchor: What to Adopt: Knowledge First ✅ ... Evidence = Knowledge ✅ ... Factive Mental States ✅ ... Non-Luminosity ✅ ... Margin for Error ✅ ... Anti-KK ✅ ... Knowledge Rule for Assertion ✅ ... What to Reject: Knowledge = Justified True Belief ❌ ... Phenomenal Evidence ❌ ... Transparency of Rationality ❌ ... Luminosity of Mental States ❌ ... Recommendation: Integrate ... into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2
rows.statement: Final recommendation table adopts all seven listed concepts (Knowledge First, Evidence=Knowledge, Factive Mental States, Non-Luminosity, Margin for Error, Anti-KK, Knowledge Rule for Assertion) unconditionally (all checked, no [PROP]/[OPEN] hedging) and recommends integrating them directly into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2 -- a materially stronger, less-hedged recommendation than the same-day review (S2528), which instead treats most of these as PROP-status research candidates and explicitly places 'Evidence=Knowledge' on its own rejection list.

sources.note: A proposed standing programme invariant (Step 291 vNext Audit H): reject any inference where the CARRIER, ABSTRACTION LEVEL, SPEECH-ACT STATUS or GOVERNANCE STATUS changes without an explicit derivation. Ten named inference patterns (e.g. PureClaimSetUnion -> the full knowledge-state algebra K, Sigma-order -> K-order, candidate -> canonical, dependency-edge -> cycle-membership, classification-closed -> membership-closed, derivable-repair-class -> one specific implementation, unblocked-analysis -> resolved-condition, bounded-family -> selected-relation, graph-leverage -> next-action) are tested and all ten rejected; six of the ten had actually been committed by Steps 287-291 themselves and are corrected by this rule.

rows.anchor: This programme has repeatedly found the same class of mistake: a true statement at level A is silently promoted to a statement at level B. ... ADD §X — CLAIM-LEVEL TYPE DISCIPLINE
rows.statement: Requires a new mandatory section formalizing 'Claim-Level Type Discipline' as a standing programme invariant: for every headline result, record source carrier, target carrier, source status, target status and inference rule, and reject any inference where carrier, semantic level, or speech-act status changes without an explicit derivation; supplies eight worked mandatory test cases (Sigma->K, PureClaimSetUnion->K, candidate->canonical, dependency->cycle, classification->membership, definition->decision-procedure, derivable->unique-implementation, unblocked->resolved).

rows.anchor: AUDIT E — IDENTITY "FORCED" CLAIM ... If multiple identity repairs satisfy the required invariants, state that the repair class is forced but the implementation is not.
rows.statement: Requires that the word 'forced' in the identity-repair finding (id = H(P,e,c,t,Pi) re-keying on withdrawal) be scoped precisely across six distinct propositions (observed failure of current construction, necessity of a revision-stable mechanism, necessity of preserving historical identity, necessity of some replacement mechanism, uniqueness of the specific proposed repair, governance authorization), and that if multiple repair formulas satisfy the invariants, the finding must be stated as 'the repair class is forced, the implementation is not.'

rows.anchor: EDGE-GENERATION RULES admitted: a cited passage states that B REQUIRES SOMETHING FROM A rejected: co-mention ... definitions: an IDENTIFICATION contributes ONE edge ... candidates: a CANDIDATE proposal is modelled as its own node ... blocked: blocked dependencies ARE included ... transitive: NOT included
rows.statement: Formally documents the graph's edge-generation rules for the first time in explicit form: an edge is admitted only when a cited corpus passage states B requires something from A (not mere co-mention); a definitional identification contributes exactly one directed edge (a prior version's bidirectional treatment was removed); a candidate/unratified proposal is modelled as its own node rather than folded into a definitional edge (the Step-290 correction to the Z-1 cycle); blocked dependencies are included as edges (blockage is a status, not an absence); transitive edges are excluded.

rows.anchor: NOT FROZEN — step-291/11_VNEXT-CLOSURE-AUDIT.md. A reviewer audit ruled "do not freeze Step 291 yet" and ran eight audits over this artifact. The substance stands; six claims are DOWNGRADED for overstatement
rows.statement: Documents, inline at the top of the headline artifact, that this version of Step 291 is explicitly NOT FROZEN and that a subsequent adversarial audit (the vNext, 8 audits) downgrades six of its claims for overstatement while confirming the underlying substance stands.

rows.anchor: AUDIT E ... The repair CLASS is forced (revision-stable identity); no specific replacement formula is entailed by the experiment. ... at least three repairs satisfy the invariants — the derivable ⇒ one-architecture leap, committed by me
rows.statement: Corrects the prior 'the repair is forced' identity finding into six separated propositions, concluding only that a revision-stable identity mechanism CLASS is forced (the current construction demonstrably fails under withdrawal, and StructuralValid plus persistent-identity principles jointly require some replacement), while the specific replacement formula is not entailed - at least three distinct candidate repairs (projecting state out of id, a surrogate key, versioned identity) each independently satisfy the required invariants, so asserting one specific formula was an unwarranted derivable-implies-unique-implementation leap.

experiment.hypothesis: the actual producer of a self-undeclared artifact can be established mechanically
experiment.setup: search all session transcripts for write-class tool_use blocks targeting the artifact path
experiment.assumptions: transcript retention exists; git commit timestamps correlate to the writing session within seconds
experiment.inputs: 33 session transcripts, one git commit
experiment.method: grep for write-class operations, exclude tool_result echoes, correlate timestamp to commit
experiment.result: exactly one session (2da45a86) issued the write; corroborated by that session's own written self-disclosure
experiment.interpretation: the producer is 2da45a86, already excluded by name in the independence bar
experiment.limitations: requires transcript retention; covers only tool-mediated acts; self-contaminating if searched naively
experiment.conclusion: SB-1's independence precondition is cleared, durably

sources.note: Step 199's invariant that correlated/derivative evidence (e.g. multiple AI agents reporting from the same underlying source) must not be counted as independent confirmation; grounds a typed Evidence Graph (derivedFrom/supports/contradicts/corroborates/supersedes) and the quantitative-estimate provenance invariant I_65.

rows.anchor: EvidenceVolume \neq EvidenceStrength. ... one highly reliable independent observation may be more valuable than 100 copies of the same unreliable observation.
rows.statement: Distinguishes the amount of evidence n(E) from its Quality(E); worked example -- if ten AI agents independently 'report' the same conclusion but all derived it from the same source (E1=E2=...=E10), the ten reports are not ten independent pieces of evidence, and naively computing P(H|E1..E10) as if independent is a classic statistical trap.

rows.anchor: I_{64}: Correlated or derivative evidence must not be counted as independent confirmation without justification.
rows.statement: New invariant I_64: correlated or derivative evidence must not be counted as independent confirmation without justification -- an important statistical governance invariant; requires preserving EvidenceProvenance and ideally EvidenceDependency (Corr(E_i,E_j)) to avoid manufacturing artificial certainty.

sources.note: The Boundary Separation Experiment: shows nine adversarial epistemic conditions (contradiction, absence, evidence-insufficiency, unobservable, underdetermined, theory-incomplete, agent-remediable, not-applicable, not-assessed) all project to the single value U yet remain pairwise distinct when represented as facet-tagged boundaries (0/36 collisions) -- but an anti-rigging test on facet keys alone finds 1 collision inside the critical six (EvidenceInsufficiency vs Underdetermined, both touching the same three facets) and an exhaustive 2^11 search finds no facet-key subset separates them; a three-value typed vocabulary for one facet (G_assessment) repairs it. Also finds 4 of 11 facets and 7 of 10 ZI invariants untestable by the nine-state suite.

sources.note: Major self-correction: re-running the D285-5/T-E witness (S2063, S2071/S2072) against all four corpus-named equality relations (not just structural/semantic/observational) reveals a FOURTH relation, provenance-sensitive (=_lambda), under which the two operations o1,o2 (differing only in provenance Pi) produce states that are NOT equal -- meaning delta IS injective on this exact witness under that corpus relation. The correct statement of what D285-5 established is therefore much weaker than originally claimed: not 'delta is non-injective' but 'delta composed with a semantic quotient that discards Pi is non-injective' -- and whether Pi should be discarded from semantic equality is itself an explicitly OPEN corpus decision (Decision 3, Step 254), meaning the original D285-5 (S2063) silently resolved an open governance/derivation question rather than deriving a settled result.

rows.anchor: E5 — WHAT DOES D285-5 ACTUALLY ESTABLISH? ... That is: non-injectivity MODULO a chosen semantic quotient. It is NOT a property of delta. Under the corpus's relation D (provenance-sensitive), the same delta IS injective on this witness.
rows.statement: Confirms, via captured executed output, the corrected/weakened statement of the D285-5 non-injectivity result (delta is non-injective only modulo a chosen semantic quotient that discards provenance, and is injective under the corpus's provenance-sensitive relation on the same witness) -- the definitive textual confirmation that the script referenced in S2081 was actually run and produced this exact result.

rows.anchor: K1={a0,a_scan[id]} via o1; K2={a0,a_vendor[id]} via o2 ... A structural = : Pi is inside id -> different ids -> different sets: VACUOUS. B semantic == : equal IF Pi is discarded -- but that CHOICE is Decision 3, OPEN: SUBSTANTIVE *but see E2*. C observational ~ : equal under cardinality-only observation: SUBSTANTIVE relative to declared set. D provenance =_lam : explicitly compares Pi -> unequal by construction: VACUOUS.
rows.statement: Re-runs the D285-5 action/result witness against all four corpus-named equality relations rather than the three previously tested, finding it vacuous under structural equality (as before), conditionally substantive under semantic equality only if a specific, currently-undecided discard-of-provenance choice is made, undefined-as-stated under observational equality pending a fixed observation set, and newly found VACUOUS under provenance-sensitive equality -- meaning two of the four relations make the property vacuous, one is conditional on an open decision, and one is undefined without further specification.

experiment.hypothesis: delta(K,o1)=delta(K,o2) does not imply o1=o2, tested against all four corpus-defined equality relations
experiment.setup: construct two Assert operations (o1 scan-origin, o2 vendor-origin) producing assertions differing only in provenance Pi, applied to base state K0={a0}
experiment.assumptions: the four corpus relations (structural/semantic/observational/provenance-sensitive) are correctly characterized from Step 246
experiment.inputs: K0={a0}; o1=(Assert,a_scan); o2=(Assert,a_vendor); four equality-relation implementations
experiment.method: compute K1,K2 under both operations and evaluate each of the four equality functions on them
experiment.result: structural: unequal (vacuous); semantic: equal only after discarding Pi (open decision); observational: equal under a cardinality-only observation set (undefined in general); provenance-sensitive: unequal (vacuous, delta is injective here)
experiment.interpretation: the property's substantive status depends entirely on which of four non-interchangeable corpus relations is chosen, and the specific choice used in the original D285-5 result was not itself corpus-justified
experiment.limitations: single witness; observational equality tested only under one arbitrarily chosen minimal observation set
experiment.conclusion: D285-5's headline conclusion must be narrowed to a claim about delta composed with a specific, corpus-underdetermined quotient, not about delta itself

rows.statement: States the precise, corrected characterization of what the D285-5 witness actually establishes: a much narrower claim than 'delta is non-injective' -- specifically, non-injectivity is a property of delta composed with a particular, not-corpus-mandated semantic quotient that discards provenance, and the very same delta is injective on the very same witness once provenance-sensitive equality (also a corpus relation) is used instead.

rows.statement: Identifies the precise mechanism of the original overreach: the corpus has an explicitly named, still-open governance decision (Decision 3, Step 254) about whether provenance/authority is part of semantic equality, and the earlier D285-5 test silently picked one answer to that open question (discard provenance) without flagging that it was making a choice at all -- meaning the result quietly substituted an assumption for an unresolved decision.

sources.note: A questioning method that reads a statistical/philosophical framework (here Stigler's pillars) as a set of protective 'anti-reasoner' functions against specific Kernel failure modes (overfitting, false certainty, mis-calibration, external bias, naive extrapolation, ignoring design, ignoring residuals), and separately lists which observations the method explicitly says should NOT influence architecture without further evidence.

rows.anchor: De Moivre's specific normal approximation ... the exact definition of Fisher information ... the specific details of the trial of the Pyx ... the details of the Cushny-Peebles data ... the French lottery example.
rows.statement: Explicitly lists five historically-important-but-architecturally-irrelevant observations that should NOT influence Kernel architecture without further evidence, distinguishing historical/mathematical detail from architectural implication.

rows.anchor: Stigler's pillars are not a theory of knowledge — they are a theory of how to extract signal from noise and manage uncertainty. ... Protects against overfitting / false certainty / mis-calibration / external bias / naive extrapolation / ignoring design / ignoring residuals.
rows.statement: Reads the seven pillars as an 'anti-reasoner' -- each pillar mapped to a protective function (against overfitting, false certainty, mis-calibration, external bias, naive extrapolation, ignoring design, ignoring residuals) -- concluding the pillars form a theory of extracting signal from noise and managing uncertainty, not a theory of knowledge, and that a Knowledge Kernel needs an analogous operation set to avoid treating data as self-evident truth.

rows.anchor: DDD treats aggregates as identity holders. But Stigler's aggregation is about discarding identity to reveal signal. ... DDD treats residuals as error. But Stigler shows that residuals are often the source of discovery.
rows.statement: Ten questions framed as blind spots of conventional DDD analysis relative to Stigler's pillars (identity-vs-discarded-identity in aggregates, equal-value-vs-diminishing-returns data, probability-as-truth-vs-calibration, generation-independent-vs-design-dependent data, residuals-as-error-vs-signal, symmetric-vs-directional relationships, valid-vs-trap extrapolation, root-n diminishing value, optional-vs-inference-creating randomization, and always-better-vs-sometimes-discard 'more data').

rows.anchor: These are not questions about missing capabilities. They are questions about the assumptions the Kernel makes about how information is extracted, calibrated, and validated from data.
rows.statement: Final ten-question architect checklist (raw-vs-aggregated data, diminishing marginal value, probability-as-truth-vs-calibration, internal-vs-external validity standards, symmetric-vs-directional relationships, generation-process awareness, residual-as-error-vs-signal, proportional-extrapolation risk, marginal-contribution weighting, first-class data reduction), explicitly framed as questions about the Kernel's assumptions rather than about missing capabilities.

sources.note: Step 194's requirement that causal claims be immutable, versioned assertions carrying full model/assumption/population/method provenance, so that model changes and refutations are traceable rather than silently overwritten; grounds a reproducibility invariant.

rows.anchor: Claim_1 \xrightarrow{superseded/refuted} Claim_2.
rows.statement: Causal claims should be immutable, versioned assertions (Claim_v1, Claim_v2=Refuted) rather than mutable fields silently overwritten (e.g. cause=deployment updated in place); a later refutation creates a new claim version linked by supersession/refutation to the original.

rows.anchor: Model_1\neq Model_2. Otherwise we cannot understand why the epistemic assessment changed.
rows.statement: When AI models evolve (Model_1 generating Claim_1, later Model_2 generating Claim_2), the architecture must preserve Model_1 != Model_2 as distinct provenance, or the reason for a changed epistemic assessment becomes unrecoverable.

rows.anchor: CausalClaim = (Proposition,Evidence,Model,Assumptions,Population,Method,Assessment,Time). This is essentially the statistical equivalent of software provenance.
rows.statement: Defines a CausalClaim schema with eight fields (Proposition, Evidence, Model, Assumptions, Population, Method, Assessment, Time), framed as the statistical equivalent of software provenance.

rows.anchor: Reproducibility is a knowledge invariant where quantitative claims matter.
rows.statement: A serious causal assertion should answer whether another qualified analyst could reproduce the assessment, requiring Data+Method+Model+Assumptions+Version to be retained; reproducibility is proposed as a knowledge invariant for quantitative claims.

sources.note: Six enumerated candidate ontological categories for what K_t represents relative to K=(𝒜,ℛ): (A) Complete knowledge state K_t=(𝒜,ℛ,Σ,...); (B) Assertion-relation state K_t=(𝒜,ℛ) with other constructs external; (C) Domain state with (𝒜,ℛ) as a projection π_K(K_t)=(𝒜,ℛ); (D) Epistemic projection K_t=π_knowledge(S_t) of a broader system state; (E) Layered model S_t=(K_t,E_t,H_t,G_t,Q_t,...) each with its own bounded context; (F) Separate products, i.e. the two models are not meant to describe the same system. Framed explicitly as 'no model shall be selected by intuition'.

rows.anchor: Model A — Complete knowledge state K_t=(𝒜,ℛ,Σ,...) ... Model B — Assertion-relation state K_t=(𝒜,ℛ) ... Model C — Domain state, π_K(K_t)=(𝒜,ℛ) ... Model D — Epistemic projection K_t=π_knowledge(S_t) ... Model E — Layered model S_t=(K_t,E_t,H_t,G_t,Q_t,...) ... Model F — Separate products ... No model shall be selected by intuition.
rows.statement: Enumerates six mutually exclusive candidate ontological categorizations (A-F) of what K_t represents relative to K=(𝒜,ℛ), explicitly stating none may be selected 'by intuition' — reframes 'which K looks better' as 'what ontological category does K represent'.

rows.anchor: A K_t=(A,R,Sigma,...) complete: REFUTED, ratified K_t contains Action/Event/Policy, which the verification lane puts OUTSIDE K. B K_t=(A,R), rest external: REFUTED, contradicts FA-4. C (A,R)=pi_K(K_t) projection: HOLDS. D K_t=pi_knowledge(S_t): HOLDS, compatible with C. E S_t=(K_t,E_t,H_t,G_t,Q_t) layered: HOLDS, compatible with C. F separate products: REFUTED, Relation and Proposition are shared primitives.
rows.statement: T-B model discrimination: of the six candidate K-relationship models (A-F) proposed in the sibling Step 285 protocol documents, this executed test REFUTES three (A complete-state, B assertion-relation-with-rest-external, F separate-products) and finds three mutually COMPATIBLE (C projection, D epistemic-projection, E layered-model) -- the first concrete, code-executed narrowing of the six-model hypothesis space in the entire sub-series, though it does not yet select a single model among C/D/E.

rows.anchor: The Knower/state boundary does not decide between K_t and (𝒜,ℛ) — both exclude the Knower. It confirms the layered shape (Model E) and eliminates nothing. Recorded so it is not later cited as evidence for a state choice it cannot support.
rows.statement: Explicitly bounds the scope of the Knower-boundary finding: since both competing K candidates (the ratified K_t and the verification-lane (A,R)) already exclude the Knower, this result cannot be used to adjudicate between them -- it only reinforces the general layered-model shape (Model E), and the document proactively warns against a later misuse of this finding as decisive evidence for a specific K choice.

rows.anchor: | **A** `K_t = (𝒜,ℛ,Σ,…)` complete | 🔴 **REFUTED** | ratified `K_t` contains `Action/Event/Policy`; the verification lane puts all three **outside** `K` | ... | **B** `K_t = (𝒜,ℛ)` | 🔴 **REFUTED** | FA-4 ... | **C** `(𝒜,ℛ) = π_K(K_t)` | ✅ **HOLDS**, qualified | ... | **F** separate products | 🔴 **REFUTED**
rows.statement: Executes the six-model evaluation (A-F) using named test scripts (exec/t285_reconcile.py T-A/T-B, exec/t285_equality.py): Model A (complete-state identity) REFUTED because ratified K_t contains Action/Event/Policy while the verification lane places all three outside K; Model B (K_t=(A,R)) REFUTED per FA-4 (K_t is state over 8 primitives, not 2); Model C ((A,R)=πK(K_t)) HOLDS, qualified, because every verification-only item is a field of an assertion, not a new primitive; Model D and Model E hold, compatible with C (reversed vantage / naming the complement); Model F (separate products) REFUTED since Relation and Proposition are shared between both models.

experiment.hypothesis: One of six candidate models (A-F) correctly characterizes the relationship between the verification-lane (A,R) and the ratified K_t.
experiment.setup: exec/t285_reconcile.py (tests T-A, T-B) and exec/t285_equality.py, evaluated against FA-4 and the verification lane's own externality declarations.
experiment.assumptions: FA-4 (K_t is state over the 8 ratified primitives) is taken as ground truth.
experiment.inputs: The ratified 8-primitive K_t definition and the verification lane's (A,R) vocabulary.
experiment.method: Primitive-set arithmetic comparison of each model's claim against FA-4 and declared externalities.
experiment.result: A, B, F refuted; C holds (qualified); D, E hold as compatible restatements of C.
experiment.interpretation: (A,R) is best understood as a qualified semantic projection of K_t, not an alternative or complete definition.
experiment.limitations: No Gita input used; result depends on the declared drop of Event/Policy/Action.
experiment.conclusion: Outcome C (lossy semantic projection) is the surviving model.

rows.statement: Distinguishes three information pathways that must not be conflated: (A) Model Knowledge -- implicit, non-traceable, non-governed LLM parametric output, to be interpreted but never treated as authoritative; (B) External Retrieval -- explicit, traceable, but ungoverned source material, a candidate-evidence source only; (C) KnowledgeOS Knowledge -- explicit, traceable, governed, versioned Epistemic State, the sole authoritative representation.

sources.note: Step 175 gives the series' most rigorous formalization yet of the recurring Chapter-4 continuity theme, explicitly borrowing the statistical concept of identifiability: a parameter/history is identifiable from an observable/current-state only if distinct values always produce distinct observables (H1!=H2 => Current(H1)!=Current(H2)); real KnowledgeOS-like systems generally violate this, illustrated by a minimal numeric counterexample (History A: 100->80; History B: 120->80; both yield CurrentState=80 but differing prior states), proving History->CurrentState is many-to-one and its inverse is not uniquely defined -- 'historical state is not identifiable from current state alone.' Frames the state transition as an information-reducing projection S=Projection(H) (if |H|>|S| in information content, multiple histories collapse to one state), and gives the concrete KnowledgeOS illustration: 'Architecture Status=APPROVED' alone reveals nothing about who proposed it, what evidence existed, which version was reviewed, or which determination/authorization supported it.

rows.anchor: S_0=100. History A: 100→80. History B: 120→80. The current state is identical: S_1=80. But: S_0^A ≠ S_0^B. ... History→CurrentState is many-to-one. ... Historical state is not identifiable from current state alone.
rows.statement: Proves via a minimal numeric counterexample (History A: 100->80; History B: 120->80, both yielding CurrentState=80 but different prior states S_0) that the mapping History->CurrentState is many-to-one, so its inverse (reconstructing history from current state) is not uniquely defined -- 'historical state is not identifiable from current state alone.'

experiment.hypothesis: the current state alone can be used to reconstruct the historical state that produced it
experiment.setup: two histories A (100->80) and B (120->80) that both terminate at CurrentState=80
experiment.assumptions: the state-transition function need not be invertible
experiment.inputs: the two synthetic histories
experiment.method: compare S_0 across both histories given identical current state
experiment.result: S_0^A != S_0^B despite Current(H_A)=Current(H_B)
experiment.interpretation: history is not identifiable from current state alone -- a formal, statistics-style identifiability failure, not merely a metaphor
experiment.limitations: toy numeric example, not a KnowledgeOS implementation test
experiment.conclusion: an architecture must not assume CurrentState implies CompleteHistory

notations: State compression can destroy epistemic information
pi(H1)=pi(H2) while H1!=H2 => S cannot distinguish histories

sources.note: Step 167's information-theoretic strengthening of the recurring state-vs-history theme: models current state as a projection of history S_t=pi(H_t) where H_t=(S_0,e_1,S_1,...,e_t,S_t); in general S_t is not equivalent to H_t (current state is a projection of history, not the complete history), and since a projection generally satisfies I(S;H) < H(H) (loses information unless injective), if pi(H1)=pi(H2) while H1!=H2 then current state cannot distinguish those two materially different histories, so state compression can destroy epistemic information (e.g. status=APPROVED alone cannot reveal who approved it, under what authority, using which knowledge/evidence/determination/policy). Concludes this mathematically validates treating lineage as a first-class architectural concern rather than merely an audit preference, without requiring full event sourcing as an implementation consequence -- the conceptual distinction (History->Projection) holds regardless of implementation.

notations: Decision=Approved must not silently become Authorization=Granted

sources.note: Step 178 states the strong invariant 'no semantic transformation may occur implicitly across bounded-context boundaries': Determination=Feasible must not silently become Decision=Approved (an explicit governance act is required), and Decision=Approved must not silently become Authorization=Granted (an explicit authorization process is required). Specifically warns AI agents are prone to collapsing these layers (reasoning 'evidence suggests the change is safe -> therefore execute it'), requiring the full chain Evidence->Determination->Governance->Authorization->Execution even when an AI participates at every step; restates AIRecommendation != GovernanceDecision (an AI's RecommendedAction=A and Governance's Decision=B can both be valid, separate artifacts). Also explicitly notes non-implication both ways: Determination=Feasible does not force Decision=Proceed (Feasible does not imply ShouldProceed), and Determination=Risky does not force Decision=Reject (governance may accept risk under explicit authority) -- yielding the corrected relation Knowledge->DecisionBasis (never Knowledge=>Decision directly), and Decision=GovernanceFunction(DecisionBasis,Norms,Constraints,Authority).

sources.note: Proposes representing observation/evidence streams as measures over time (Dirac-measure sums mu_O=sum w_i*delta_{t_i}, mu_E=sum alpha_i*delta_{t_i}) rather than assuming continuous availability, since organizational knowledge is event-like (a discovery, a board decision, a correction each occur at a point in time); explicitly keeps EvidenceWeight != TruthProbability (alpha_i is evidential contribution, not probability of truth). Introduces a five-dimensional evidential quality vector q(e)=(relevance,authority,freshness,independence,reproducibility) in [0,1]^5 and an evidential functional Phi(E,p) explicitly NOT automatically a probability, just an evidential assessment. Formalizes the correlated-evidence problem as an evidence-dependence matrix D_ij=Dependence(e_i,e_j) that aggregation must account for, particularly important for AI-generated knowledge where many 'sources' may derive from one original. Proposes an evidence measure space M_E=(E,Sigma_E,mu_E) as the mathematical foundation for evidence aggregation without forcing binary true/false, while keeping the epistemic state itself categorical: S(p,t) in {Unknown,Observed,Supported,Refuted,Conflicted,Determined,Superseded} -- states, not probabilities (an inference can produce Hypothesized but not automatically Supported).

sources.note: Imprecise-probability formalism: a representor (set of probability distributions) yielding lower/upper probability bounds, the Interval Requirement (every intermediate value between two attained credences is itself attained by some distribution in the representor), Convexity of the representor set, and Dilation (an interval widening after conditionalizing on new evidence, worked example [0.6,0.75] -> [5/6,8/9]).

rows.statement: A representor is a set of probability distributions inducing an interval cr(P) in [lower cr(P), upper cr(P)]. The Interval Requirement demands every value strictly between two attained credences also be attained by some distribution in the representor; Convexity requires the representor closed under mixtures; Dilation is the phenomenon of an interval widening after conditionalizing on new evidence, illustrated numerically ([0.6,0.75] widening to [5/6,8/9] after learning A superset R).

rows.statement: Section 17 (self-dated 'AMENDED 2026-09-06', referencing a K9-closure computation performed elsewhere): reports that once the K9 closure was actually computed, Qualify is NOT robust to the choice of capability basis -- excluded from Closure(K4) but included in Closure(K9) only because C-7 IS the qualification capability and seeds it directly, so that inclusion 'carries no evidential weight on its own' (a degenerate-estimand-style failure); the same computation found closure size ranging 15-22 of 29 constructs across 14 tested worlds, so the kernel requirement set's size is not determined by the corpus, with only five constructs (Identity, InvariantReg, K, Proposition, Relation) surviving every tested axis; explicitly still not a kernel and still not a minimality proof; downgrades the O_core-root claim to basis-robust but mapping-fragile.

sources.note: The biological-communication analogue of the G_t != K_t distinction, using a signal/receiver model; extends the graph-not-equal-state distinction from S2813.

rows.anchor: Animal communication research distinguishes the signal itself from what the receiver can infer from it. ... Signal != Information != Evidence != Knowledge. ... The receiver does not receive the predator itself. It receives Signal and constructs some internal state K^receiver_t. ... G_world != G_sign
rows.statement: Proposes animal communication (e.g. vervet monkey alarm calls) as a research lens for KnowledgeOS's Observation->Signal->Information->Assessment->Action transition, extracting the chain Signal!=Information!=Evidence!=Knowledge; models a predator encounter with the world's environmental graph, the transmitted signal, and the receiver's constructed internal state as three distinct objects (G_world != G_signal != K^receiver_t), directly echoing and reinforcing the earlier G_t != K_t distinction, since the receiver never receives the predator itself, only a signal from which it constructs meaning with evidence/uncertainty/provenance/standards.
